To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the vibrational energy of highly vibrationally excited carbon dioxide produced by photodissociating organic peroxides is efficiently redistributed to other modes of carbon dioxide and to the solvent modes.

the relaxation of the highly excited carbon dioxide molecules is caused by the near resonance energy transfer to solvent molecules and is not due to collisional energy transfer between carbon dioxide molecules.
the vibrational energy transfer between CO2 and the solvent molecules is the dominant relaxation mechanism in CH2Cl 2 and CCl 4.

the vibrational relaxation of highly excited carbon dioxides in different solvents.
the vibrational relaxation and spectroscopy of carbon dioxide produced by the photodisscociation of organic peroxy radicals in solution.
the dynamics of vibrationally highly-excited molecules in solution and the influence of solvents on the relaxation of the vibrational energy of the solute molecule.

the relaxation of the bend and symmetric stretch mode of carbon dioxide is fast, whereas the relaxation of the high frequency asymmetric stretch mode is considerably slower.

the relaxation of highly vibrationally excited carbon dioxide in solution occurs via a combination of energy redistribution between different vibrational modes of CO2 and energy transfer from the CO2 modes to the surrounding solvent.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the relaxation rates obtained by NEMD are in good agreement with the Landau-Tiller relaxation rates, which suggests that the NEMD approach can provide a useful alternative to the EMD approach for the study of the relaxation processes in highly excited molecular systems.

the relaxation of highly vibrationally excited carbon dioxide in the presence of solvent is dominated by near resonant vibrational energy transfer to solvent molecules, and that this process can be modeled with molecular dynamics simulations.
